opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, partly because my own thinking on it has shifted quite a bit over the years.

When I started out in NLP, the standard picture was a pipeline: first you figure out the syntactic structure of a sentence, then you build a logical form or meaning representation on top of that, and only then do you connect it to the world, whether that's a database, a robot's environment, or a set of images. Syntax was the scaffolding, and understanding came at the end.

What I've come to believe is that the relationship runs in both directions, and that it's much less modular than that picture suggests. On one hand, structure clearly matters. Compositionality is real. The way you put words together determines what you mean, and any system that interprets language reliably has to be sensitive to that structure in some form. On the other hand, a lot of what we used to think of as syntactic decisions, like where a prepositional phrase attaches or how to resolve some ambiguity, can't really be made without knowledge about the world. You know that "I ate the pizza with a fork" and "I ate the pizza with anchovies" have different structures because you know things about forks and anchovies, not because of anything in the grammar.

So I no longer think of parsing as a prerequisite that you finish before understanding begins. It's more that structural analysis and world modeling are interleaved, and constrain each other.

The other big change, honestly, is that the success of large language models forced a lot of us to reconsider whether explicit syntactic representations need to be built in at all. These models are trained with no supervised parse trees, and yet when you probe their internal representations, you find something that looks a lot like syntactic structure. They seem to discover it because it's useful for predicting text. That's interesting, because it suggests that structure is something that emerges from the pressure to model language and, indirectly, the world that language describes, rather than something that has to be handed to the system.

But I'd be careful not to overcorrect. The fact that structure emerges doesn't mean it's unimportant, and there are still clear cases where models fail at systematic, compositional generalization in ways that look like a failure to really use structure. So the question I find most interesting now isn't "do we need parsing?" but "what kinds of representations, structural and otherwise, do these systems actually build, and how do those connect to a model of the world that they can reason about and act in?" That's where I think a lot of the exciting work is right now.

r001.rationale: The response says many attachment and ambiguity decisions depend on knowledge about the world, not just grammar, illustrated by forks versus anchovies.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that text corpora lack sufficient co-occurrence evidence to resolve scene-dependent ambiguities.

r003.rationale: It describes world modeling and interleaved structure, but does not propose mentally simulating the described scene as the way people resolve ambiguity.

r004.rationale: It does not claim that scene simulation requires prior visual experience of the objects.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and honestly my answer has changed a lot over the years. When I started out, I think I had this picture, and a lot of the field had this picture, where parsing was the thing you did first. You get a sentence, you recover its syntactic structure, that gives you something like a logical form, and then the logical form is what you ground in the world. Syntax was the scaffolding for meaning. And a lot of my early work on semantic parsing, on instruction following, was really built on that assumption: if you can get the structure right, understanding sort of falls out.

What I think now is that the arrow points the other way at least as often. If you look at what current models do, they don't seem to need an explicit parse to do most of the things we used to think required one. And yet when you probe them, there's a lot of structure in there that looks syntactic. So I've come to see syntax less as a prerequisite for understanding and more as a kind of compression of regularities in how the world gets described. The reason languages have the constituency structure they have is partly because the world has parts and relations, and agents and patients, and events that unfold in time. Syntax is a shadow cast by that structure onto the sequence of words.

So the relationship I'd describe now is something like: parsing and world modeling are two views of the same underlying problem. If you have a good model of situations, a lot of syntax becomes predictable. And if you've internalized enough syntax, you've implicitly learned a lot about what kinds of situations are possible. Where it gets interesting, and where I think there's still real work to do, is the cases where those two things come apart. Models that have great syntactic competence but bizarre beliefs about physical or social reality, or models that can track a world state in some narrow domain but can't describe it compositionally. Those failures are what tell you syntax and understanding aren't literally the same thing, even if they're deeply coupled.

I guess the short version is: I used to think of parsing as a tool for building a world model. Now I think of it as evidence about what the world model already contains, and I'm much more interested in what it means for a system to be able to act on that structure than in whether it can draw the tree.

r001.rationale: The response discusses syntax and world modeling generally but does not identify inadequate world knowledge, rather than inadequate grammar knowledge, as the source of many parsing errors.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss text corpora, co-occurrence evidence, or scene-dependent syntactic ambiguity.

r003.rationale: It does not propose mentally simulating a described scene as a way to resolve ambiguity.

r004.rationale: It does not connect scene simulation to prior visual experience of the objects involved.

astra-6.text:
I think parsing is an important piece of language understanding, but it’s not a self-contained problem in quite the way we sometimes treated it. The structure of a sentence helps you figure out who did what to whom, what’s being asserted, and how the meanings of the parts fit together. But figuring out that structure can itself require knowing something about the world—what events are plausible, what the speaker is trying to communicate, and what’s already happened in the conversation.

So I see the relationship as going in both directions. You use syntax to build an interpretation, and you use your understanding of the situation to resolve uncertainty about the syntax. That doesn’t mean syntactic structure stops being useful, or that every language system needs a separate parser. It means that producing a parse tree isn’t the endpoint of understanding. The interesting question is how that structure helps you connect an utterance to the world and to the intentions of the person who said it.

r001.rationale: The response says world knowledge can help resolve syntactic uncertainty, but does not identify inadequate world knowledge as the source of many parsing errors or contrast it with inadequate grammar knowledge.

r002.rationale: It makes no claim about text corpora or insufficient co-occurrence evidence.

r003.rationale: It says situation understanding can help resolve syntactic uncertainty, but does not propose mentally simulating the described scene.

r004.rationale: It does not connect scene simulation to prior visual experience of the objects involved.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I now see syntax as one piece of a much larger problem. When I started working on language, it was tempting to think that if we could recover the right structure of a sentence—figure out what modifies what, who did what to whom—we would have done a substantial part of understanding it. And that structure is useful. But it doesn’t, by itself, tell you what the sentence means in the world.

If I say, “The trophy wouldn’t fit in the suitcase because it was too big,” syntax gets you some of the way, but figuring out what “it” refers to requires knowing something about objects and containment. So the relationship goes both ways: linguistic structure helps you organize what someone is telling you about the world, and your understanding of the world helps you figure out the structure and interpretation of what they said.

That makes me less inclined to think of parsing as a separate stage that you finish before understanding begins. I’m more interested in how those things can be learned and used together.
